issues.legal_issue: The disputed sale was not a bona fide and genuine transaction and did not confer title on the purchasers.
material_facts: The company’s board resolution recorded a consideration of Rs.5,000, while a director later received Rs.7,000; the record did not explain the increase.
The resolution was not mentioned in the receipt, the agreement to sell, or the sale deed, and the evidence supported the finding that it had been antedated.
The agreement to sell and the sale deed were not in terms of the resolution, and the agreement recited a sale for Rs.7,000 despite evidence that the amount had already been paid.
The purchasers did not exercise ownership rights over the property before filing suit; the company maintained it for the directors’ use until the statutory vesting date.
The sale was between the company and the directors’ wives, who had no independent source of income.
Although the resolution, payment, and sale deed were proved, the court found that the circumstances and intrinsic evidence showed the transaction was not bona fide or genuine.
issues.conclusion: The sale was neither bona fide nor genuine and conferred no right on the purchasers.
issues.legal_principle: The genuineness of a transaction is assessed from the evidence and the circumstances as a whole, including intrinsic inconsistencies and the parties’ conduct. A transaction that is not bona fide and genuine does not confer title. The court relied on the evidence discussed in the judgment and, on vesting, on Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. Madanlal Agrawal, (1997) 1 SCC 177.

rule.if: civil_title_claim_challenging_a_property_sale and sale_to_directors_relatives and (resolution_inconsistent_with_sale_documents or unexplained_consideration_change) and company_retained_use and purchasers_did_not_exercise_ownership

predicates.civil_title_claim_challenging_a_property: The proceeding is a civil title claim in which a disputed sale of property is challenged.
predicates.sale_to_directors_relatives: A company sold property to persons related to its directors.
predicates.resolution_inconsistent_with_sale_docume: The company’s recorded sale resolution was not reflected in later documents relating to the sale.
predicates.unexplained_consideration_change: The amount ultimately recorded or paid differed from the amount in the company’s resolution without an explanation.
predicates.company_retained_use: The company continued to maintain or use the property after the purported sale.
predicates.purchasers_did_not_exercise_ownership: The purchasers did not act as owners of the property before bringing their claim.

issues.definition: When a civil title claim concerns a company sale to directors’ relatives, and the sale documents are inconsistent or the consideration changes without explanation while the company retains use and the purchasers do not exercise ownership, the purchasers acquire no title.

issues.legal_issue: A court may look behind a company’s separate personality to determine whether a sale to directors’ relatives was genuine or a transaction between the relatives behind the company’s separate identity.
material_facts: The property was sold by a company to the wives of its directors, who were brothers.
The opposing party alleged that the sale was sham and collusive and had been made to prevent the property from vesting under the nationalisation legislation.
The court considered the relationship between the directors and purchasers alongside the other circumstances bearing on the transaction’s genuineness.
issues.conclusion: The court was justified in piercing the corporate veil to ascertain the real parties to the sale and whether the transaction was genuine and bona fide.
issues.legal_principle: The separate legal personality of a company is a basic incident of incorporation, as recognised in Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.; however, courts may pierce the corporate veil to examine the realities behind that personality. The court relied on that principle in assessing whether the sale was genuine.

predicates.company_property_transaction_challenged_: A transaction involving company property is alleged to be sham or collusive.
predicates.sale_to_directors_relatives: The company transferred property to persons related to its directors.

issues.definition: When a transaction involving company property is challenged as sham and the transfer is to directors’ relatives, the court may pierce the corporate veil.

issues.legal_issue: A party relying on a disputed transaction must first establish that it is bona fide and genuine; only then must the opposing party prove that it is sham or fictitious.
material_facts: The purchasers relied on the board resolution, a receipt for payment, and the executed sale deed to establish their claim.
The court found that the circumstances and intrinsic evidence did not establish that the transaction was bona fide and genuine.
The opposing party’s alleged failure to produce rebuttal evidence did not require a finding in favour of the purchasers once their initial burden had not been met.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers did not establish that the sale was bona fide and genuine, so it was unnecessary to determine whether the opposing party had separately proved that it was sham, bogus, or fictitious.
issues.legal_principle: A party attacking a transaction as sham, bogus, or fictitious bears the burden of proving that allegation, but where the issue also asks whether the transaction was bona fide and genuine, the party relying on the transaction must first prove that it was. Only after that initial showing must the opposing party dislodge it.

predicates.dispute_over_genuineness_of_a_transactio: The parties dispute whether a transaction is bona fide and genuine or sham and fictitious.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_transaction_for_title: The claimant relies on the transaction as the basis of a claim to title.
predicates.claimant_evidence_does_not_establish_bon: The evidence presented by the claimant does not establish that the transaction was bona fide and genuine.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a disputed transaction for title but does not establish its bona fides, the opposing party need not prove that the transaction was sham.

issues.legal_issue: Property that remained owned by a scheduled coal company on the appointed date vested in the Central Government under the nationalisation legislation.
material_facts: The company that owned the property was included in the schedule to the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973.
The court found that the purported sale to the purchasers was not bona fide or genuine, so the property remained the company’s property.
The Act came into force and the property vested on the appointed date; the vested properties were thereafter transferred to the government company.
issues.conclusion: Because the sale conferred no right on the purchasers, the property remained the company’s and vested in the Central Government under Section 3(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3(1), read with Section 2(h)(xi) and the relevant schedule entry, the rights, title, and interest of the owners of scheduled coal mines vested in the Central Government on the appointed date. The court also relied on Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. Madanlal Agrawal, (1997) 1 SCC 177.

predicates.nationalised_coal_property_case: The proceeding concerns whether property associated with a coal company vested under coal nationalisation legislation.
predicates.owner_was_scheduled_coal_company: The company owning the property was included in the legislation’s schedule.
predicates.no_genuine_transfer_before_vesting: No bona fide and genuine transfer removed the property from the company’s ownership before statutory vesting.

issues.definition: When a scheduled coal company owned the property and no genuine transfer occurred before vesting, the property vests in the Central Government.
